question: After a cement mill baghouse pulse-valve replacement, compressed-air use rises but cleaning pulse counts remain unchanged. How can a plant research agent distinguish valve seat leakage, pulse duration, receiver pressure recovery and shared-header demand before authorizing a valve purchase?
category: Baghouse pulse-valve leakage and shared compressed-air header attribution
scenario: Higher compressor loading after maintenance with unchanged PLC pulse count
evidence_required: Valve part numbers, diaphragm and seat inspection, manufacturer-rated pressure and pulse duration
Time-aligned PLC output waveform, receiver pressure recovery, header flow and compressor kW at matched production
Isolation test under approved lockout and pressure-safety procedure, leak survey and other consumers on shared header
answer_and_decision_guide: Compare matched operating periods and check whether compressor metering includes unrelated users. Confirm actual solenoid energization duration and valve closure, rather than equating pulse count with air mass. Use pressure-decay or flow evidence under an authorized safe isolation procedure to separate seat leakage from control timing and other users. Do not prescribe a universal pulse setting or bypass dust-control protection.
source_provenance: Seller-maintained discovery page is not a validated valve OEM manual; installed valve datasheet and plant records are required.
free_first_decision: Review existing maintenance, PLC, compressor and leak-survey records before buying any replacement valve or digital reference.

conditional_paid_check.authorization: Verify exact file or component specification, edition, usage rights and quoted price; require explicit buyer approval; no autonomous purchase.

model_limitations: Without isolated flow, timing and header allocation measurements, no reliable leakage quantity or savings estimate is possible.
